title: How Inscribe uses generative AI to improve document classification and fraud detection (in any language)
summary: See how Inscribe improved document classification coverage and quality by evolving our system with a hybrid AI pipeline.
body_markdown:
Correctly identifying a document's type is a key part of[AI fraud detection](https://www.inscribe.ai/fraud-detection/ai-fraud-detection) .


Each type (bank statement, payslip, utility bill, invoice, and more) carries different context and data, which influences which fraud checks are run.


At Inscribe, we’ve supported document classification for years, but recently we took a major leap forward. By incorporating generative AI into our pipeline, we significantly improved both how many documents we classify and how accurately we do it.


### **Improving on a strong foundation**


Our original document classification system was built in-house using traditional machine learning. It learned to recognize patterns that distinguish, say, a bank statement from a utility bill. The system was accurate and robust, but it had growing limitations, especially as we expanded globally.


First, our training data was overwhelmingly in English, so performance dipped for non-English documents. That was a problem as our customers increasingly process international applications.


Second, while we supported an "UNKNOWN" type for unclassifiable or irrelevant documents (like selfies, pet photos, and vacation snapshots), we found that some documents that *should* have been classifiable weren’t being picked up, limiting our classification coverage.


Third, we lacked a streamlined way to add support for new document types. Expanding the system was possible, but slow and manual.


### **Enter generative AI**


While we’ve continuously maintained and improved our ML system, major leaps required more than just tweaks. Generative AI gave us a way to accelerate meaningful improvements, without spending months curating new training datasets.


Our new hybrid pipeline combines the strengths of traditional ML, large language models (LLMs), and visual language models (VLMs):


- **Non-English documents** now bypass our original system entirely and are classified directly with an LLM, which understands the document content via text.
- **English-language documents** still use our original system – except when the result is UNKNOWN. In that case, we pass it through an LLM for a second opinion. **‍**
- **All remaining unclassified documents** , both English and non-English, go through a VLM. This model can analyze the visual content of documents, which is especially useful when the text alone is sparse or unhelpful.


VLMs are slower and more expensive, so we use them selectively, as a final step to reduce the UNKNOWN rate without impacting performance.


### **The impact**


Since launching this improved pipeline on April 3, we’ve seen significant gains, especially for non-English documents. Their classification rate increased by 19%. English documents also improved. Given that some documents truly don’t fit any supported type, we’re confident we’re approaching the practical ceiling for classification.


Since this launch, document fraud has only accelerated: Inscribe's 2026 State of Document Fraud Report found that AI-generated document fraud grew[nearly 5x](https://www.inscribe.ai/reports/2026-document-fraud-report) between April and December 2025, and 97.8% of the fraud and risk leaders we surveyed said they're concerned about AI-enabled document fraud. Because generative AI is now one of the primary tools fraudsters use, generative AI-powered classification remains a core building block of effective[AI fraud detection for lenders.](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/ai-fraud-detection-for-lenders)


The classification work described here has also grown well beyond a single step. Our[AI Agents for document fraud detection](https://www.inscribe.ai/product/overview) now run a multi-model pipeline where classification is one stage in a larger investigation: fast initial parsing, entity extraction, and cross-document analysis all reasoning together the way a fraud analyst would, with a full assessment returned in[under 90 seconds](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/how-inscribe-uses-amazon-bedrock-to-stop-document-fraud-in-seconds/) . It's the same generative AI capability described below, now built into a larger agentic system for[generative AI fraud detection.](https://www.inscribe.ai/fraud-detection/generative-ai-fraud)


Classification is just the first step. Once we know what a document is, parsing it accurately matters just as much: our team applied this same generative AI approach to bank statement parsing, boosting non-English account number coverage from 18% to 94% and customer name coverage from 80% to 94% (see[how LLMs boosted our bank statement parsing coverage](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/how-llms-boosted-our-bank-statement-parsing-coverage-by-up-to-5x) by up to 5x).


Even more exciting, this allows us to identify new document types we hadn’t previously supported. When an LLM returns something like “marriage certificate” or “medical record,” it gives us insight into what else users are uploading and helps us prioritize future expansions to our supported types.


Understanding what a document *is* lays the foundation for detecting what’s *wrong* with it. That’s why classification is so critical, and why we’re so excited about this progress. Generative AI isn’t just helping us detect fraud better; it’s helping us understand our data better. And that opens the door to smarter, faster, and more inclusive fraud detection going forward. For a broader look at how generative AI is reshaping document fraud, see[our analysis of deepfakes and document fraud in the age of generative AI.](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/from-forgeries-to-deepfakes-document-fraud-in-the-age-of-generative-ai)
